title: Trust the Man
full_review:
A sterling cast is wasted in the tepid and often coarse comedy-drama "Trust the Man" (Fox Searchlight) about an insecure actress, Rebecca (Julianne Moore), who has taken a break from films to star in a play at New York's Lincoln Center.

It's clear that she and her house-husband, Tom (David Duchovny), are having some marital problems, especially in the intimacy department, as they tell their marriage counselor (Garry Shandling).

Rebecca's slacker brother ,Tobey (an especially good Billy Crudup), lives with his longtime girlfriend, Elaine (Maggie Gyllenhaal), an aspiring writer. The relationship has been coasting along for seven years, but now Elaine decides she wants to get married and have a baby, and the commitment-phobic Tobey -- who's obsessed with death -- can't handle it.

Before long, Tom falls under the spell of Pamela (Dagmara Dominczyk), a predatory mother he meets when picking up his child from school. And when Tobey and Elaine come to a parting of the ways, Tobey falls under the sway of former girlfriend Faith (Eva Mendes), now married.

Writer-director Bart Freundlich's film offers the occasional sharp observation about modern-day relationships, but the characters' infidelities and casual attitude toward sex is highly problematic, despite the morally sound wrap-up, which plays out in an improbable but amusing scene on Rebecca's opening night.

Moore, Duchovny, Crudup, and Gyllenhaal are all pros, and watching them in anything has its rewards, but even from a dramatic standpoint there is something phony about the setup, and inasmuch as this is also a comedy genuine chuckles are few.

The film contains much rough language, a few instances of profanity, needlessly frank sexual talk, premarital and adulterous relationships, a casual approval of pornography, a couple of sex scenes without nudity, some gratuitous scatological elements and a same-sex kiss. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
